sources.source: Exponential Backoff And Jitter (AWS Architecture Blog)

items.item: N clients compete in the first round, N-1 in the second round, and so on, and the no-jitter approach is the clear loser on both work and time
idempotency keys are up to two hundred fifty-five characters long and are pruned after at least twenty-four hours (API v1)

sources.source: Scaling your API with rate limiters (Stripe engineering blog)

items.item: Stripe uses the token bucket algorithm to do rate limiting, with a bucket per user

Offset pagination re-reads a row when an insert shifts later rows into the position the next fetch reads, and skips a row when a delete shifts later rows out of a position the next fetch would have read — both measured directly against identical mutations.

A keyset cursor eliminates the re-read entirely, because it names a row's own identity rather than a position an insert can shift — but it cannot recover a row deleted before the cursor ever reaches it, which is the same blind spot a hard delete leaves for any cursor.

A token-bucket limiter's 429 response can carry the exact wait until a token exists again; a client that reads and obeys that number wastes close to the fewest calls mathematically possible, measured directly against a client guessing with a short fixed delay.

at.step: Reveal: obeying the wait time, measured

items.item: Fixed exponential backoff keeps every losing client retrying on the same schedule, so the same group of clients collides again on the same later round; adding randomness breaks that synchronization and measurably reduces both total requests and time to completion, reproducing the AWS Architecture Blog's own experiment.

An idempotency key turns a write into something as safe to repeat as a read: the same key retried three times against a real mock endpoint recorded exactly one underlying charge and returned the identical response every time.

An OAuth authorization server is free to rotate the refresh token on a successful refresh and invalidate the old one immediately, so two workers racing on the identical stale token cannot both succeed — a shared lock serializing the two attempts removes the race entirely, both measured directly.

Rotating a client secret the same abrupt way would recreate the identical outage shape; the documented fix is accepting two valid secrets at once during a transition window rather than a hard cutover.

Chapter 4 topic 9's resilient-client patterns (timeouts, retries, backoff) are applied here to a whole ingestion loop under rate limiting rather than re-taught from scratch; topic 3's high-watermark-cursor vocabulary (naming identity instead of position) reappears as the keyset fix, not re-derived independently.
